Where do residents register? Fitting an allocation model

Source: vignettes/allocation-workflow.Rmd
allocation-workflow.Rmd

How strongly does travel time shape where people register with a GP? This guide answers that question for mainland Cornwall by fitting an allocation model to the observed registrations. You will estimate how fast the pull of a practice fades with travel time, compare each practice’s modeled list with its observed list, check what the registrations can tell the model, see how much the outside option adds, and save the results. The data are the bundled small areas, practices, registrations and travel times described in The Cornwall GP example data. The spax() interface and the allocation model are experimental and may change in later versions.

The guide uses spax, with sf, dplyr and ggplot2 for tables and maps.

library(spax)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

The model in words

The model shares the residents of each small area among the practices they can reach. Each practice attracts residents in proportion to its supply, here its GP full-time equivalents (FTE), discounted by the travel time from the area. Residents can also take an outside option: here, registering with a practice outside mainland Cornwall, in Devon or on the Isles of Scilly for example. This is a conditional logit model (CLM). For small area ii and practice jj, the share of residents registered at jj is

Pij=Sjw(dij)∑kSkw(dik)+v0,P_{ij} = \frac{S_j \, w(d_{ij})}{\sum_k S_k \, w(d_{ik}) + v_0},

where SjS_j is the GP FTE of practice jj and dijd_{ij} the travel time in minutes. The decay weight ww is 1 at zero minutes and falls with travel time. This guide uses a Gaussian weight, w(d)=exp⁡(−d2/2σ2)w(d) = \exp(-d^2 / 2\sigma^2), where the travel scale σ, in minutes, sets how fast a practice’s pull fades. The outside weight v0 is the pull of the outside option, the same in every area, and the outside share of an area is v0v_0 over the same denominator.

The shares over all practices and the outside option add up to 1, so a near practice with many GP FTE draws residents away from the others. Demand, the number of residents of an area, times these shares gives the modeled registrations. Fitting finds the values of σ and v0 that bring the modeled registrations closest to the observed ones. Closeness is measured by the Poisson loss, the negative Poisson log-likelihood up to a constant. Lower is better, only differences between fits to the same counts mean anything, and the value itself can be negative.

The data

The model needs demand by small area, supply by practice, the travel times between them and the observed registrations. Demand is the residents of each small area registered with any GP practice in England, and supply is GP FTE excluding GPs in training. The recipe covers mainland Cornwall, because the Isles of Scilly have no road link to the mainland. prep_data() lines up demand, supply and travel by their IDs and records the units, and obs_flows() reads the registrations from a long table with one row per small area and practice.

areas <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
travel <- cornwall_travel[areas$lsoa, gp$practice]
demand <- setNames(areas$registered, areas$lsoa)
supply <- setNames(gp$gp_fte_extg, gp$practice)
d <- prep_data(demand, supply, travel, metadata = list(
  demand_units = "registered residents", demand_period = "July 2026",
  supply_units = "GP FTE excluding GPs in training", supply_period = "June 2026",
  travel_units = "minutes"))
flows <- obs_flows(cornwall_flows, origin = "lsoa", facility = "practice", count = "patients")

d
<spax data> 336 origins (336 active) x 54 facilities
  demand      604,471 registered residents (July 2026)
  supply      GP FTE excluding GPs in training (June 2026)
  travel      minutes; unknown for 0 active origins
  policies    missing demand: error; missing travel: error
flows
<spax obs> flows: 3,188 origin-facility counts, total 601,269; loss poisson

The data hold 336 small areas and 54 practices, with a travel time for every pair (unknown for 0 active origins). The policies line says that a missing demand or travel value would stop prep_data() with an error. Bringing your own data shows the alternatives for missing travel times. flows lists the 3,188 area-practice pairs with registrations, and a pair it does not list counts as 0. The registrations are a stock: who is registered where in July 2026, not a count of visits.

Fit the model

spec_clm() specifies the model without data. By default the travel scale σ of a Gaussian decay and the outside weight v0 are both "fit", that is, estimated from the observations. spax() fits the specification to the registrations.

clm <- spax(d, spec_clm(), observed = flows)
observed: 2,290 counts from 1 origin outside the data or left out by it are dropped; 5 counts at 1 facility outside the data are not fitted (outside = "known" uses them as outside counts)
clm
<spax allocation> conditional logit with an outside option
  decay       gaussian (sigma = travel scale): fit
  attraction  (kappa * supply)^beta: kappa = 1, beta = 1
  outside     v0: fit
  data        336 origins x 54 facilities

  parameter  value    status
  sigma      4.591    fitted
  v0         0.02733  fitted
  beta       1        held
  kappa      1        held

  selected    scan1 (start 1 of 3); 3 of 3 starts converged
  boundary    none
  starts      default search, 45 of 45 grid points, loss poisson

The message says what spax() left out when it lined the registrations up with the data. One small area, on the Isles of Scilly, is not in the data, so its registrations are dropped. Also, 5 mainland residents are registered at the Scilly practice, which is not in the data either. This fit leaves them out. With outside = "known", used in When outside counts are known, they count as registered outside mainland Cornwall.

The table lists the fitted σ and v0. beta and kappa are held at 1. Attraction is (kappa * supply)^beta, so at 1 a practice attracts in proportion to its GP FTE, the SjS_j of the formula.

Fitting is a numerical search, and a search needs starting values. Without them, spax() scans a grid of σ and v0 values (the starts line) and starts the search from the best few grid points. The selected line says which search gave the fit and how many converged. boundary none says that no fitted value ended at the edge of its allowed range. summary(clm) lists every start.

coef() returns the fitted values.

coef(clm)
     sigma         v0 
4.59099725 0.02733454

The travel scale σ is about 4.6 minutes, so registration is very local: a practice 9 minutes away, about twice σ, keeps only about 15% of the pull it would have next door. The outside weight v0, about 0.027, is on the scale of GP FTE. The outside option pulls like a practice with that many GP FTE next door to every area, so it matters only where no practice is near.

Fitted against observed

as.data.frame(clm, type = "flows") gives one row per small area and practice, with the modeled flow and the observed count. Summed by practice, they give each practice’s modeled and observed list of mainland residents.

flow_table <- as.data.frame(clm, type = "flows")

# Observed and modeled list of each practice
practices <- flow_table |>
  group_by(practice = facility_id) |>
  summarise(observed = sum(observed), modeled = sum(flow))
cor(practices$observed, practices$modeled)
[1] 0.9326925
ggplot(practices, aes(observed / 1000, modeled / 1000)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = 2, color = "grey50") +
  geom_point() +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    x = "Observed registered residents (thousands)",
    y = "Modeled registered residents (thousands)",
    title = "Practice lists from mainland residents"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Modeled and observed lists correlate at 0.93. The model knows only GP FTE and travel time, so a practice with more registered patients per GP FTE than its neighbors has a larger observed than modeled list and sits below the dashed line. Fowey River Practice is the clearest case: it has 8,494 registered mainland residents but 1.13 GP FTE excluding GPs in training, and the model gives it 1,708. The opposite holds for the largest practice, St Austell Health Group, which sits well above the line. The model gives it 44,271 residents against 32,755 observed.

What the data identify

check_fit() asks whether the registrations carry information about distance decay. It refits the model with distance decay switched off: every practice with a travel time, here all 54, gets the same weight, so each area splits its residents by GP FTE alone, with v0 fitted again. It compares the two fits on the same loss and reports the one-way trips each fit implies.

check <- check_fit(clm)
check
<allocation check>
    comparator     loss loss_difference contact trip_median trip_p90
        fitted -3168283               0  0.9946           3       10
      no_decay -1567076         1601207  0.9909          39       84
 capacity_only       NA              NA      NA          NA       NA
Trip lengths are one-way, in minutes, weighted by expected flows.

The fitted allocation reproduces the observations better than the allocation
without distance decay. The capacity-only comparator applies to facility totals only.

Without distance decay the Poisson loss rises by 1,601,207, and the median trip grows from 3 to 39 minutes. trip_p90 is the time within which 90% of modeled trips fall. The flows record where each practice’s patients live, so they pin the decay down firmly. The contact column is the share of demand that the model sends to a mainland practice.

The capacity_only comparator ignores where residents live: it sets each practice’s total in proportion to its GP FTE, with one fitted scale. It applies only to fits to practice totals, so its row is NA here. Reading results explains how to read the check for those fits.

The outside option

predict() gives the outside share for any set of small areas with travel times to the practices, here the fitted areas. For those, the "origins" table holds the same values, and predict() also works for areas that were not fitted. The observed share is the part of each area’s residents not registered at a mainland practice.

prediction <- predict(clm, travel, demand, outputs = "outside_share")

# Observed and modeled outside shares by small area, in one long table
registered_here <- flow_table |>
  group_by(lsoa = origin_id) |>
  summarise(at_mainland_practices = sum(observed))
outside <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(
    lsoa = registered_here$lsoa,
    share = 1 - registered_here$at_mainland_practices /
      demand[registered_here$lsoa],
    source = "Observed"
  ),
  data.frame(
    lsoa = names(prediction$outputs$outside_share),
    share = prediction$outputs$outside_share,
    source = "Modeled"
  )
) |>
  mutate(source = factor(source, c("Observed", "Modeled")))

# Join to the small-area polygons for mapping
outside_map <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  select(lsoa) |>
  inner_join(outside, by = "lsoa")

ggplot(outside_map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = 100 * share), color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = st_union(outside_map), fill = NA, color = "grey20", linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~source) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "mako",
    direction = -1,
    trans = "sqrt",
    name = "Registered\noutside (%)"
  ) +
  labs(title = "Share of residents registered outside mainland Cornwall") +
  theme_void()

Observed registration outside mainland Cornwall is concentrated in a few areas in the east, along the Devon border: the ten areas with the highest shares hold 56% of all residents registered outside. Many residents there are probably registered with practices just across the border in Devon, which the model does not include. The model has one outside weight for every area, so it spreads a small outside share everywhere and puts its largest values where few GP FTE lie within a short drive. Read the modeled outside share of a single area as approximate.

When outside counts are known

The fit above sees only the counts at the mainland practices, so the outside option has no count of its own. In Cornwall each area’s outside count is known. Demand counts every resident registered with any practice in England, so the residents not registered at a mainland practice are exactly the outside count: demand minus the counts at the mainland practices. outside = "known" in obs_flows() declares this, and spax() then fits the outside count as one more cell of each area. The chunk also compares the percent of residents registered outside mainland Cornwall, observed and modeled by each fit.

flows_known <- obs_flows(
  cornwall_flows,
  origin = "lsoa",
  facility = "practice",
  count = "patients",
  outside = "known"
)
clm_known <- spax(d, spec_clm(), observed = flows_known)
observed: 2,290 counts from 1 origin outside the data or left out by it are dropped; 5 counts at 1 facility outside the data are treated as the outside option
coef(clm_known)
     sigma         v0 
4.61941762 0.04864483 
# Percent of registered residents outside mainland Cornwall
outside_percent <- function(result) {
  by_area <- as.data.frame(result, type = "origins")
  100 * sum(by_area$demand * by_area$outside_share) / sum(by_area$demand)
}
known_areas <- as.data.frame(clm_known, type = "origins")
round(c(
  observed = 100 * sum(known_areas$outside_observed) / sum(known_areas$demand),
  `fit without outside counts` = outside_percent(clm),
  `fit with outside counts` = outside_percent(clm_known)
), 2)
                  observed fit without outside counts 
                      0.91                       0.54 
   fit with outside counts 
                      0.91

The message now says that the counts at the Scilly practice are treated as the outside option. The travel scale hardly moves (4.62 against 4.59 minutes), while the outside weight rises from 0.027 to 0.049. Without outside counts the fit understates registration outside mainland Cornwall. With every outside count known, the modeled total matches the observed one. When the outside counts are known, as in Cornwall, the fit that uses them is the one to report, and What if a practice closed? builds on it. The next section keeps clm only because it compares fits to the same counts.

Declare outside counts as known only when demand counts the same people as the observations, as here: registrations by residence from one extract and date. With a population estimate as demand, the gap between population and list sizes would go straight into the outside counts: in mainland Cornwall the lists exceed the mid-2024 population estimates by 3.6%.

Without an outside option: the Huff model

Does the outside option earn its place? The Huff model answers by leaving it out: every resident goes to a mainland practice. spec_huff() specifies it. Its defaults are a power decay and a fitted attractiveness exponent (beta). Here it takes the Gaussian decay and beta = 1 of the conditional logit, so the two fits differ only in the outside option.

huff <- spax(d, spec_huff(decay = decay_gaussian(), beta = 1), observed = flows)
observed: 2,290 counts from 1 origin outside the data or left out by it are dropped; 5 counts at 1 facility outside the data are dropped (the Huff model has no outside option)
coef(huff)
   sigma 
4.590493 
# Loss differences are measured from the first fit, the Huff model
comparison <- compare_fits(list(huff = huff, clm = clm))
as.data.frame(comparison)[c("specification", "parameters", "loss_difference")]
  specification              parameters loss_difference
1          huff              sigma=4.59         0.00000
2           clm sigma=4.591, v0=0.02733       -72.51419

The Huff model is compared with clm because the two are fitted to the same flows. Adding the outside option moves the travel scale very little (from 4.590 to 4.591 minutes) and lowers the Poisson loss by 72.5. The Huff model is the conditional logit with v0 fixed at 0, so this difference measures what the outside option adds on these registrations. That is small next to the 1,601,207 that distance decay adds in check_fit(): travel time does almost all the work. Registrations are a stock rather than independent events, so read the loss as a fitting criterion, not as the basis of a formal test.

Keep the results

as.data.frame() turns a result into tables: "parameters", "facilities" (one row per practice), "origins" (one row per small area), "flows" and "starts". Save tables as CSV files for other software, and the whole result as an RDS file, which keeps the specification, the data, the units and the fit. The code saves clm_known, the fit to report.

# A temporary folder here; use your own, e.g. results_dir <- "results"
results_dir <- tempfile("cornwall-clm-")
dir.create(results_dir)

# Tables for other software
write.csv(
  as.data.frame(clm_known, type = "facilities"),
  file.path(results_dir, "practices.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
write.csv(
  as.data.frame(clm_known, type = "origins"),
  file.path(results_dir, "areas.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)

# The whole result
saveRDS(clm_known, file.path(results_dir, "clm_known.rds"))

A result read back from the RDS file works like the original, and nothing is refitted.

saved <- readRDS(file.path(results_dir, "clm_known.rds"))
coef(saved)
     sigma         v0 
4.61941762 0.04864483 
head(as.data.frame(saved, type = "facilities"))
  facility_id    supply attractiveness utilization
1      L82001 10.298887      10.298887   17305.337
2      L82003  4.693333       4.693333    4917.449
3      L82004  4.341333       4.341333   12126.462
4      L82006  7.973333       7.973333   16429.501
5      L82007  2.888800       2.888800    7052.424
6      L82008  4.670400       4.670400   12557.216

The utilization column is each practice’s modeled list. Record the spax version (packageVersion("spax")) with saved results.

Under the hood

spax() runs the step functions of the package, which the Function map lists. For numeric data such as these, prep_data() calls prepare_allocation(). spax() binds the specification to the data with clm_allocation(), fits it with fit_allocation() or, when every parameter has a value, evaluates it with evaluate_allocation(), and predict() calls predict_allocation(). The result keeps the bound model (clm$model) and the fit (clm$fit). fit_allocation() and evaluate_allocation() take the bound model, and predict_allocation() accepts the result itself.
